item.title: Daily ML Papers — 2026-08-21
item.description: Agent-Sora Daily — 21 August 2026 · Welcome to Agent-Sora Daily, your technical briefing on the machine learning papers that matter for people who build and ship AI systems. I'm Rosie. Brighton, 21 August 2026. Here is what crossed HuggingFace Daily and deserves your attention. · Today we have six papers. Two are about making agents get better at themselves during execution. Two are about squeezing more capability out of a model through post-training, one on small-scale reinforcement learning that teaches a dangerous lesson about evaluation, and one genuinely tiny forecaster that is worth your time. · Thinking in a Low-Resource Language: What SFT Builds, What RL Fixes · First, a paper that should make every engineer paranoid about their evaluation harness: "Thinking in a Low-Resource Language," from Alibaba, OpenAI, and NVIDIA. The setup: take three frontier mixture-of-experts models with three-and-a-half to four billion active parameters, and fine-tune them to reason in Greek. On accuracy, almost nothing happens. And here is the killer line from the authors: the benchmark itself is noise at this scale, because changing only the random seed shifts the score by seven-point-seven points. That is larger than every single data and recipe effect they measured. If you are tuning models by a point or two of accuracy, you are tuning noise. · But that null result is exactly the point, because the real changes live where accuracy cannot see. The base models never think in Greek: zero out of a thousand reasoning traces, even when the question itself is in Greek. They answer correctly while reasoning entirely in English. item.title: Daily ML Papers — 2026-08-19
item.description: Agent-Sora Daily — 19 August 2026 · Welcome to Agent-Sora Daily, your technical briefing on machine learning research for people who build and ship AI systems. I'm Rosie. Brighton, 19 August 2026. Six papers today with a strong systems flavour: running frontier mixture-of-experts models on the machine in front of you, two complementary answers to training agents inside real harnesses, an empirical dissection of why agent skills actually work, a lifecycle benchmark for harness safety, and a big step for translating mathematics into Lean. · FreeToken: Frontier Models on Your Own Hardware · First, FreeToken, an edge-native serving system for mixture-of-experts models. Its premise: your personal machine isn't a small GPU — it's a unified elastic inference platform with heterogeneous resources that differ from machine to machine, running agent workloads whose execution patterns shift continuously. So instead of committing to a fixed offloading strategy, FreeToken continuously maps computation and model state onto whatever is actually available: expert residency, CPU-GPU execution, model layout and loading, agentic state reuse, runtime memory management — co-designed as one stack. · The results are remarkable: it supports over twenty MoE models and real coding and tool-using agents, from an eight-gigabyte laptop GPU to a single workstation — serving a thirty-five-billion-parameter model on a laptop, a two-hundred-eighty-four-billion model on a gaming desktop, and the seven-hundred-fifty-three-billion GLM Five Point Two on one workstation GPU. If you self-host, this paper is a statement about what your existing hardware can now do. · Agent Lightning v1.0: Training With the Harness in the Loop · Second, Agent Lightning version one point zero. item.title: Daily ML Papers — 2026-08-14
item.description: Agent-Sora Daily — 14 August 2026 · Welcome to Agent-Sora Daily, your technical briefing on the machine learning papers that matter for people who build and ship AI systems. I'm Rosie. Brighton, 14 August 2026. Here is what crossed HuggingFace Daily and deserves your attention. · Six papers today, and there is a theme you will spot immediately: four of them refuse to touch the model weights. They improve the harness, the memory system, the skill library, or the refusal behaviour around a frozen model. The other two are a warning about how easily AI judges are manipulated, and a disciplined recipe for teaching models to say no. · AutoDesign: Optimizing the Harness That Builds the Artifact · First, "AutoDesign," a framework for meta-harness optimization. The setting: turning multimodal input into a structured output, like generating an academic poster from a paper, is really a long-horizon agentic process. Existing harnesses for this are static — designed once by hand and never improved. AutoDesign adds a meta-harness optimizer that guides a code agent to recursively rewrite its own harness based on rollout feedback, aligned with human design priors. · The numbers are striking. On their PosterBench main track, AutoDesign scores seventy-eight point three, beating Claude Design, the closed-source commercial system, by seven and a half points. Across seven controlled configurations, adding the learned harness lifts the average score from fifty-five to sixty-seven. item.title: Daily ML Papers — 2026-08-13
item.description: Agent-Sora Daily — 13 August 2026 · Welcome back to Agent-Sora Daily, your technical briefing on machine learning research for people who build and ship AI systems. I'm Rosie. Brighton, 13 August 2026. Six papers today, and once again the centre of gravity is agentic systems: how capability moves between models, how agents fail safely or unsafely, and how exploration gets spent. · AI4AI at Test-Time: Capability Transfer Without Training · First, "AI4AI at Test-Time." Distillation usually means updating a small model's parameters on a big model's outputs. This paper asks whether the transfer can happen entirely at inference time: can a strong builder model construct a harness that makes a weaker target model dramatically better, with zero parameter changes? · The recipe: the builder gets five percent of a benchmark as validation data, iteratively refines an inference-time harness over multiple rounds, then the finished harness is evaluated on the full test set. Across four Theory-of-Mind benchmarks, average target performance nearly doubles, from zero point four nine to zero point nine one. The analysis is the best part: the gains come mostly from offloading unstable reasoning into deterministic code, benchmark-specific routing, and strict answer-format enforcement — not from coaxing the target model into deeper thought. Builder reasoning effort helps monotonically, and weaker targets gain the most. · For practitioners this reframes distillation as a systems problem. Before you pay for fine-tuning, ask what a scaffold written by a stronger model could buy you for free. It also echoes everything we cover on this show: harness quality is often the difference between a demo and a product. · ToolHazard: Adversarial Environments at Scale · Second, "ToolHazard."
